name: Manute Bol
milestone_by_age_26: Drafted by the Washington Bullets in the 1985 NBA draft and set a franchise record with 12 blocked shots in a single game during his rookie season, leading the NBA in blocks per game.
early_history_summary: Bol grew up as a Dinka tribesman in rural Sudan and began playing basketball around age 16. He was discovered by American coach Don Feeley at a Sudanese national team clinic in 1982, came to the U.S. to play at Division II University of Bridgeport in 1984, and entered the NBA draft after one year of college.
family_context_summary: Born to a Dinka tribal family in rural South Sudan; his father was a herder in the village of Gogrial. Family financial background not documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: extreme height, mentor connection, Division II college
evidence_summary: Bol's extraordinary 7'7" frame was his primary advantage, discovered by American coach Don Feeley at a Sudanese national team clinic in 1982. After one year at Division II Bridgeport where he averaged 22.5 points and 13.5 rebounds, Bol entered the NBA and set a rookie franchise record for blocks in a single game. His path from rural Sudan to the NBA was driven almost entirely by his physical uniqueness rather than years of training.
starting_point: Born to a Dinka tribal family in rural South Sudan; father was a herder in the village of Gogrial in the savanna country west of the Sudd.
current_position: Died June 19, 2010 in Charlottesville, Virginia at age ~48; final role was humanitarian activist and former NBA player.

trajectory.event: Enrolled at University of Bridgeport and began playing college basketball in the United States as a Division II All-America selection.
Drafted by Washington Bullets in the 1985 NBA draft; set franchise record with 12 blocks in a single game during rookie season.
Led the NBA in blocks per game (5.0) during his rookie season, the highest rookie average in league history.
Traded to the Golden State Warriors, continuing his NBA career.
Played final NBA season, ending a 10-year career with more blocked shots than points scored.
Died on June 19, 2010 in Charlottesville, Virginia from kidney failure and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

name: Zinaida Turchyna
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Champions Cup with Spartak Kyiv in 1970 (age 24), part of a dominant run of 13 consecutive European titles, and won the first of 20 consecutive USSR Championships in 1969.
early_history_summary: Turchyna was introduced to handball at age 13 by coach Ihor Turchyn, who later became her husband. She joined Spartak Kyiv at age 16 and quickly became a star, winning the first of 20 consecutive USSR Championships in 1969 at age 23.
family_context_summary: Born in Kyiv, Ukraine (then Soviet Union); married her coach Ihor Turchyn at age 19 in 1965. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Spartak Kyiv, coach-husband Turchyn, early start at 13, Soviet sports system
evidence_summary: Turchyna was brought to handball at age 13 by coach Ihor Turchyn, who became her husband and lifelong mentor. She joined Spartak Kyiv at 16 and won the first of 20 consecutive USSR Championships at 23, followed by the first of 13 European Champions Cups at 24. The Soviet sports system and the dominant Spartak Kyiv club provided an elite performance pipeline that concentrated opportunity.
starting_point: Born in Kyiv, Ukraine (then Soviet Union); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from coaching in 1996; serves as president/manager of Spartak Kyiv; named best female handball player of the 20th century by the IHF in 2000.

trajectory.event: Introduced to handball by coach Ihor Turchyn and began playing for HC Spartak Kyiv.
Married coach Ihor Turchyn and began competing for the Soviet national team.
Won the first of 20 consecutive USSR Championships with Spartak Kyiv.
Won the first European Champions Cup with Spartak Kyiv, beginning a run of 13 titles.
Won Olympic gold medal at the Montreal Olympics with the Soviet team.
Won second Olympic gold medal at the Moscow Olympics.
Named best female handball player of the 20th century by the International Handball Federation.

name: Miklós Németh
milestone_by_age_26: Won javelin gold at the 1970 Summer Universiade in Turin with a throw of 81.94m at age 24, and competed at the 1966 European Championships finishing fifth at age 20.
early_history_summary: The son of 1948 Olympic hammer throw champion Imre Németh, Miklós initially trained as a high jumper before switching to javelin in his teens after a serious injury. He joined the Hungarian national team in 1965 at age 19 and competed at his first European Championships in 1966.
family_context_summary: Son of Imre Németh, 1948 Olympic hammer throw champion. Growing up in an Olympic champion's household provided direct exposure to elite athletics from birth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Imre Németh was an Olympic gold medalist in the hammer throw (1948), providing direct domain expertise in throwing events.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Olympic champion father, Hungarian national team, throwing sports tradition
evidence_summary: Németh grew up as the son of 1948 Olympic hammer throw champion Imre Németh, providing direct domain exposure and athletic infrastructure from childhood. He joined the Hungarian national team at 19, competed at the 1966 European Championships at 20 finishing fifth, and won Universiade gold at 24. His father's Olympic legacy created both pressure and opportunity in throwing events.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungary; son of Imre Németh, 1948 Olympic hammer throw champion.
current_position: Retired from competitive athletics; worked as coach, javelin designer, and vice-president of the Hungarian Athletics Federation.

trajectory.event: Joined the Hungarian national athletics team.
Finished fifth in javelin at the European Athletics Championships in Budapest.
Won javelin gold at the Summer Universiade in Turin with a throw of 81.94m.
Won Olympic gold medal in javelin at Montreal with a world record throw of 94.58m.
Designed a new serrated-tail javelin model that set world records before being banned by the IAAF in 1991.
Elected vice-president of the Hungarian Athletics Federation.

name: Kim Ki-duk
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Kim worked in factories from age 15 and did not begin engaging with film until age 30 when he moved to Paris; his first feature film was released in 1996 at age 36.
early_history_summary: Kim grew up in a rural area of Gyeongsangbuk-do, South Korea, and after graduating from elementary school worked in factories from age 15. He moved to Paris at age 30 to study art, where he first encountered cinema. He won a screenplay contest in 1995 and directed his first film, Crocodile, in 1996.
family_context_summary: Born in Bong-hwa, Gyeongsangbuk-do, South Korea; family owned rice paddies in Ilsan. Limited formal education, leaving school after elementary school.
evidence_summary: Kim Ki-duk had no material milestone by age 26. He left school after elementary education and worked in factories from age 15, including in a button factory, junkyard, and electronics factory. He did not encounter cinema until age 30 in Paris, and his first feature film was released at age 36. His later success as a filmmaker was entirely a post-26 phenomenon.

name: Alfred Swift
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic silver medal in the 4,000m team pursuit at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics at age 21, and gold in the track time trial at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games at age 23.
early_history_summary: Swift grew up in Durban, South Africa, and discovered cycling as a teenager through the local racing scene. He earned provincial colours for Natal and later Transvaal, and received his Springbok colours in 1952, the same year he competed at his first Olympics.
family_context_summary: Born in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: provincial cycling, local racing scene, Springbok colours
evidence_summary: Swift emerged from Durban's local cycling culture, earning provincial colours before being selected for South Africa's national team. He won Olympic silver at 21 in the team pursuit at Helsinki and later added Commonwealth gold in 1954 and Olympic bronze in 1956. Limited documentation exists about his family background or early training environment.
starting_point: Born in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died April 13, 2009 in Johannesburg, South Africa at age 77; final role was former president of the South African Cycling Federation.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic silver medal in the 4,000m team pursuit at the Helsinki Olympics.
Won gold in the track time trial at the British Empire and Commonwealth Games in Vancouver.
Won Olympic bronze medal in the 1,000m time trial at the Melbourne Olympics.
Captained the South African team at the Rome Olympics.
Died on April 13, 2009 in Johannesburg, South Africa.

name: Tony Roche
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1966 French Open singles title at age 21, defeating István Gulyás in straight sets; also won Grand Slam doubles titles and the Davis Cup with Australia from 1965 at age 20.
early_history_summary: Roche grew up in Tarcutta, a small town in New South Wales, and started playing tennis at age 9. His father, a butcher, and mother were recreational tennis players who encouraged his interest. He was coached by legendary Australian coach Harry Hopman, who also mentored Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall.
family_context_summary: Born in Tarcutta, New South Wales, Australia; father was a butcher and both parents were recreational tennis players who encouraged his interest from age 9.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were recreational tennis players who encouraged Roche's interest from childhood; father worked as a butcher.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harry Hopman coaching, Australian tennis system, Newcombe doubles partnership, tennis family
evidence_summary: Roche started tennis at 9 in a small Australian town, encouraged by recreational tennis-playing parents. He was coached by Harry Hopman, the legendary Australian Davis Cup coach who also mentored Laver and Rosewall. By 20, Roche was a Grand Slam doubles champion and Davis Cup winner; at 21, he won the French Open singles title. His partnership with John Newcombe in doubles became one of the greatest teams of the 20th century.
starting_point: Born in Tarcutta, New South Wales, Australia; son of a local butcher, with parents who were recreational tennis players.
current_position: Retired tennis player and coach; coached world No. 1 players including Ivan Lendl, Patrick Rafter, Lleyton Hewitt, and Roger Federer; resides in Turramurra, New South Wales.

trajectory.event: Won Grand Slam doubles titles and Davis Cup with Australia; runner-up at French Open singles.
Won the French Open singles title at Roland Garros, defeating István Gulyás in straight sets.
Turned professional with World Championship Tennis; leading money winner on WCT tour; Wimbledon runner-up to Rod Laver.
Achieved world No. 2 ranking; US Open singles runner-up to Rod Laver.
Won Davis Cup with Australia, defeating Adriano Panatta in a crucial singles match.
Inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame alongside John Newcombe.

name: Jean-Pierre Jarier
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Formula One Grand Prix debut at the 1971 Italian Grand Prix at Monza at age 25, and finished third in the 1970 French Formula Three Championship at age 24.
early_history_summary: Jarier grew up near Paris in a family that operated a small hotel. He discovered the Montlhéry racing circuit near Paris and began racing motorcycles before convincing his mother to sell her Peugeot to fund a Renault 8 Gordini. He progressed through Formula France and French Formula Three before moving to European Formula Two.
family_context_summary: Grew up in the Paris suburbs in a family that operated a small hotel. His mother sold her Peugeot road car to fund his first racing car.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family operated a small hotel; no motorsport background documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Montlhéry circuit proximity, family hotel, Formula France pipeline, mother's car sale
evidence_summary: Jarier grew up near Paris with access to the Montlhéry racing circuit, which sparked his motorsport career. His mother sold her Peugeot to fund his first racing car, a Renault 8 Gordini. He progressed through Formula France and French F3, finishing third in the 1970 championship, before making his F1 debut at Monza in 1971 at age 25.
starting_point: Born in Charenton-le-Pont, near Paris; family operated a small hotel.
current_position: Retired from Formula One racing after the 1983 season; specific current status not documented in reviewed sources.

trajectory.event: Finished third in the French Formula Three Championship with a Tecno-Ford.
Made Formula One debut at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza with Shell-Arnold team.
Dominated the European Formula Two championship with eight wins and raced full-time in Formula One with March.
Joined Shadow Racing Cars in F1; finished third at Monaco Grand Prix after death of teammate Peter Revson.
Took pole position for the opening two rounds of the F1 season but mechanical failures denied him victory.
Competed in his final Formula One season, ending a 12-year F1 career with 135 Grand Prix starts.

name: Paolo Borsellino
milestone_by_age_26: Passed the magistracy competition and became the youngest magistrate in Italy in 1962 at age 22, later serving as a judge at the Tribunal of Enna from 1965.
early_history_summary: Borsellino grew up in the Kalsa neighborhood of Palermo, Sicily, in a middle-class family. His father was a pharmacist and his mother ran a pharmacy. He studied law at the University of Palermo, graduating in 1962, and immediately passed the magistracy competition to become Italy's youngest magistrate.
family_context_summary: Born in the Kalsa neighborhood of Palermo to a middle-class family; father was a pharmacist and mother ran a pharmacy in Via della Vetriera.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family ran a pharmacy; no legal or judicial background documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: University of Palermo, middle-class family, Palermo justice system, Falcone collaboration
evidence_summary: Borsellino grew up in a middle-class Palermo family that ran a pharmacy, in the Kalsa neighborhood where the Mafia was present but quiescent. He graduated in law from the University of Palermo in 1962 and immediately passed the magistracy competition, becoming Italy's youngest magistrate at 22. His childhood friendship with Giovanni Falcone and proximity to Palermo's justice system shaped his career trajectory toward anti-Mafia work.
starting_point: Born in the Kalsa neighborhood of Palermo, Sicily; father was a pharmacist and mother ran a pharmacy.
current_position: Killed by a car bomb on July 19, 1992 in Via D'Amelio, Palermo at age 52; final role was prosecuting magistrate and anti-Mafia judge.

trajectory.event: Graduated in law from the University of Palermo and passed the magistracy competition, becoming Italy's youngest magistrate.
Assigned as judge to the Tribunal of Enna in Sicily.
Transferred to the Tribunal of Palermo and joined the criminal investigation office under Rocco Chinnici.
Began working on Mafia-related cases after the killing of Captain Emanuele Basile in Monreale.
The Maxi Trial of 1986-87 resulted in 360 convictions of Mafia defendants, largely due to the work of Borsellino and Falcone.
Killed by a car bomb in Via D'Amelio, Palermo on July 19, 1992, two months after the assassination of Giovanni Falcone.

name: David Ruelle
milestone_by_age_26: Completed a PhD in physics at the Free University of Brussels in 1959 at age 24, with the thesis prepared at ETH Zurich under Res Jost, and became a Privatdozent at ETH Zurich by 1961.
early_history_summary: Ruelle was born in Ghent, Belgium, and studied civil engineering for two years in Mons before switching to physics at the Free University of Brussels. He prepared his PhD at ETH Zurich under Res Jost, completing it in 1959 at age 24, then served as Research Assistant and Privatdozent at ETH Zurich.
family_context_summary: Born in Ghent, Belgium. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: ETH Zurich, Free University of Brussels, Res Jost supervision, IAS Princeton
evidence_summary: Ruelle was born in Ghent and studied engineering before switching to physics at the Free University of Brussels. He completed his PhD at 24 under Res Jost at ETH Zurich, then became a Privatdozent at ETH before being invited to the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton at 27. His trajectory through elite institutions in mathematical physics was remarkably rapid.
starting_point: Born in Ghent, Belgium; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Emeritus professor at the Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques (IHES) in Bures-sur-Yvette, France, since 2000; distinguished visiting professor at Rutgers University.

trajectory.event: Completed PhD in physics at the Free University of Brussels, with thesis prepared at ETH Zurich under Res Jost.
Became Privatdozent at ETH Zurich after serving as Research Assistant.
Appointed professor at the Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques (IHES) in France.
With Floris Takens, coined the term 'strange attractor' and developed a new theory of turbulence.
Awarded the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics.
Awarded the Dirac Medal for contributions to mathematical physics.

name: Angelina Jolie
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Girl, Interrupted (1999) at age 24, after winning Golden Globe Awards for George Wallace (1997) and Gia (1998).
early_history_summary: Jolie was born in Los Angeles to actor Jon Voight and actress Marcheline Bertrand. She made her screen debut at age 7 in Lookin' to Get Out (1982), trained at the Lee Strasberg Theater Institute, and began her professional film career with Cyborg 2 (1993) at age 18. Her breakthrough came with the HBO film Gia (1998), for which she won a Golden Globe.
family_context_summary: Born in Los Angeles to Academy Award-winning actor Jon Voight and actress Marcheline Bertrand. Her brother James Haven is also an actor and director.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Jon Voight is an Oscar-winning actor; mother Marcheline Bertrand was an actress and model. Both parents were in the film industry.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Jon Voight daughter, Hollywood royalty, Lee Strasberg training, LA film industry, industry access from birth
evidence_summary: Jolie was born into Hollywood royalty as the daughter of Oscar-winning actor Jon Voight and actress Marcheline Bertrand. She made her screen debut at 7, trained at the Lee Strasberg Institute, and grew up immersed in the film industry in Los Angeles. Her inherited network and domain exposure gave her early access to auditions, training, and industry connections that most actors spend years building. By 24, she had won an Academy Award for Girl, Interrupted.
starting_point: Born in Los Angeles to Academy Award-winning actor Jon Voight and actress Marcheline Bertrand; raised in the film industry from birth.
current_position: Academy Award-winning actress, filmmaker, and humanitarian; former UNHCR Special Envoy; estimated net worth ~$120 million; resides in Los Angeles.

trajectory.event: Made screen debut alongside father Jon Voight in Lookin' to Get Out.
Began professional film career with leading role in Cyborg 2.
Won Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actress for the HBO film George Wallace.
Won Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Girl, Interrupted, after winning Golden Globe for Gia.
Starred as Lara Croft in Tomb Raider, establishing herself as a leading lady in blockbuster films.
Starred in Mr. & Mrs. Smith, a major commercial success.
Directed and co-starred in Unbroken; starred in Maleficent, her highest-grossing film.
Directed the war drama Without Blood, continuing her filmmaking career.

name: Wole Soyinka
milestone_by_age_26: Served as dramaturgist at the Royal Court Theatre in London (1958-1959) and had his first plays, The Swamp Dwellers and The Lion and the Jewel, performed in Ibadan in 1958-1959, all by age 25.
early_history_summary: Soyinka was born in Abeokuta, western Nigeria, the son of an Anglican minister and headmaster. He attended Government College Ibadan and University College Ibadan before continuing at the University of Leeds in England, where he began writing plays and working at the Royal Court Theatre.
family_context_summary: Born in Abeokuta, western Nigeria; father was a prominent Anglican minister and headmaster, mother was a shopkeeper and local activist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was headmaster of a school, providing an educational environment; mother was a local activist. No literary background documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Government College Ibadan, University of Leeds, Royal Court Theatre, Anglican minister father, Yoruba traditions
evidence_summary: Soyinka was born to a prominent Anglican minister and headmaster in Abeokuta, Nigeria, giving him access to elite education from childhood. He attended Government College Ibadan and University College Ibadan before moving to the University of Leeds, where he began writing plays. By 24, he was dramaturgist at the Royal Court Theatre in London and had his first plays performed in Ibadan. His unique position between Yoruba traditions and Western theatre shaped his distinctive voice.
starting_point: Born in Abeokuta, western Nigeria; son of a prominent Anglican minister and headmaster and a shopkeeper mother.
current_position: Nobel Prize-winning playwright, poet, and novelist; first African Nobel laureate in Literature (1986); active writer and public intellectual at age 92.

trajectory.event: Became dramaturgist at the Royal Court Theatre in London; first plays The Swamp Dwellers and The Lion and the Jewel performed in Ibadan.
Awarded Rockefeller fellowship; returned to Nigeria and founded 'The 1960 Masks' theatre group.
Produced Kongi's Harvest and The Road, establishing himself as a major African playwright.
Arrested and imprisoned for 26 months during the Nigerian Civil War for attempting to mediate between factions.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first African laureate.
Held visiting professorships at Cambridge, Sheffield, and Yale universities.

name: Lee Chul-seung
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic bronze medal in men's doubles at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics at age 20, and gold in men's doubles at the 1992 Asian Table Tennis Championships.
early_history_summary: Lee was born in Gimcheon, South Korea, and became one of South Korea's top table tennis players in the 1990s. He graduated from Sungeui High School and attended Kyung Hee University, and was affiliated with the Samsung Life Table Tennis Club.
family_context_summary: Born in Gimcheon, Gyeongsangbuk-do, South Korea. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: South Korean table tennis system, Samsung Life club, doubles specialization, Olympic pipeline
evidence_summary: Lee emerged from South Korea's table tennis pipeline, winning Olympic bronze in doubles at 20 at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics. He was affiliated with the Samsung Life Table Tennis Club and attended Kyung Hee University. South Korea's strong table tennis infrastructure and his doubles specialization were key factors in his early success. Limited documentation exists about his family background or early training.
starting_point: Born in Gimcheon, Gyeongsangbuk-do, South Korea; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from competitive table tennis in 2005; served as coach of the South Korean men's national table tennis team.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic bronze medal in men's doubles at the Barcelona Olympics with Kang Hee-Chan; won gold at Asian Table Tennis Championships.
Won gold in men's doubles at the Asian Games in Hiroshima.
Won Olympic bronze medal in men's doubles at the Atlanta Olympics with Yoo Nam-Kyu.
Competed at the Sydney Olympics, finishing fourth in men's doubles.
Competed at the Athens Olympics, finishing fifth in men's doubles.
Retired from competitive table tennis and transitioned to coaching.
